html:
For the last twenty years, the startup path was simple: raise VC money, build software, find product-market fit, scale. Services businesses never fit the model. Services meant the customer needed something custom which involves human labour. Hence to scale a services business, you also needed to scale headcount, which didn't create the outsized leveraged returns required to live in startup land.

AI flipped this.

Software can now adapt to each user, with AI shaping the interface, meaning products can now take the job of some services. On the other side, services businesses can now have their admin and ops run by agents, meaning services can become productised (think an AI-native accounting firm). On either side, this means custom solutions can be built in a faster and more repeatable way.

Overall, this unlocks a new kind of business: a hybrid that looks like a service from the outside but runs mostly like a product - a productised service.

I'm betting on this as the next low-risk way to build a $50M+ company. I started Hourglass AI last year at 21. We sell outcomes, not software. We're bootstrapped, always profitable, and this year we had our first $100k month.

Everyone my age keeps hearing that AI is taking their grad job. I think there's never been a better time to start a business yourself. We've landed in the biggest technology boom the world has ever seen, and this is the type of business that lets anyone capitalise on it.

Software Is Becoming a Service

For twenty years, software asked you to learn it. You bought the tool, sat through the onboarding, and bent your business around how it worked. Most people had 'proficient in Excel' on their resume.

When intelligence is basically unlimited, the product can learn you instead: your business, your systems, your context. The interface reshapes itself around how you work. It is now dead simple to clone even the most complex software using AI. This is not dissimilar to the idea of a software factory - where you can now turn a customer's intent into custom software quickly. When the software itself is cheap to copy, what's left to sell is the result.

This also benefits the consumer - no one wants another tool. They want something that works for them, and someone accountable when it doesn't.

Services Are Becoming Software

At the same time, the other side is moving. When AI does most of the work, a service stops scaling with headcount. The first time you deliver something for a client, it's entirely custom. The fifth time, you notice most of it's the same, and build a recipe. The difference now is that with AI you can productise that recipe: the playbooks, the workflows, the verification steps. This now becomes the product behind your business and its moat is your distribution and all the learnings and failures it took to get there.

This leaves the team to focus on the human side, and also to push the boundaries of the business with new creative ventures.

Some people are calling this a software factory: turning a client's intent into a repeatable, custom software layer, fast. The customer still gets something built around them. You just aren't building it from scratch every time.

The Hybrid Model

So software is moving towards services, and services are moving towards software. We are now at a stage where all businesses are converging to have some layer of service to them.

This business looks like a service to the customer. They talk to a human, they get exactly what they want, built to their needs. Internally, however, the process runs like a product - a machine that spits out value. As Sequoia pointed out:

"For every dollar spent on software, six are spent on services."

This is a very big deal. The prize for business owners isn't the software budget, but the labour budget. Or, as they predict:

"The next $1T company will be a software company masquerading as a services firm."

A services business already owns the customer relationship and the outcome, it only has to productise the delivery.

Growth Over Cuts

Every week you hear in the news that jobs are being lost to AI. This implies that since AI makes things more efficient, you then cut people or resources. I heard Jensen Huang talk at Stanford in April, and he made it really clear to me why this is BS, with Nvidia being the example. Say the company writes a billion lines of code in a year. Now, with AI, it can write that in one month instead. The job-cut story assumes they'll now do the same amount of work with a tenth of the people. Instead, he argued the obvious thing for them to do is write twelve billion lines of code a year and make far more revenue. His message to young people was basically: if you're willing to go all in on AI, there's more room for you than ever.

That's where the demand for these hybrid service businesses is coming from. As Niki Scevak from Blackbird put it:

"If you improve someone's revenue, you get reflexive demand. If you save someone costs, you do not."

Are Productised Services Lucrative?

The usual pushback against services is that they're less scalable and therefore less lucrative than software-based product businesses. Services firms trade at a fraction of software multiples, because they scale with people and their margins are thin.

This isn't true of fully AI-native productised service businesses. When most of the delivery is productised, every new client costs a fraction of the last one, and the margins start to look like software. That's the whole point of the convergence: you keep the service relationship and get product economics.

Further, if you never sell the business, it will be cash-generating and profitable. The same can't be said for most software product businesses, which often require initial capital investment, and therefore a large exit to make it worthwhile for investors.

Why It's the Best First Business

If you're young and savvy with AI, I think this is the most risk-adjusted way to start a company right now:

  • You get paid straight away. Your first client pays you for work you can already do.
  • You're profitable from day one. You pay yourself out of the business, not from savings.
  • You own all of it. No investors or board required.
  • You find out what you actually want. Nobody knows what they want to do at 21. A service lets you figure it out and continually pivot whilst getting paid to learn.

The playbook is simple yet hard to do. To start, pick one niche skill you enjoy, sell the outcome to one client and deliver it yourself. Do it a few more times, learn what survives contact with real businesses, then get agents to do it. When you hit the ceiling of what you can do alone, if possible, combine forces with someone who has deep expertise and connections in the industry you're going after.

First you must make it exist, then you can make it beautiful.

Where This Goes

Once the business earns the right to exist, the creative part opens up. For us, that might mean acquiring businesses and rebuilding them around AI.

Another cool opportunity we see is to create an ecosystem so other young people can start these types of businesses. We already have AI expertise, playbooks and distribution to help them flourish.

Software is becoming a service, services are becoming software, and the businesses that meet in the middle will win the next decade.

If you want the playbooks I use to run Hourglass, they're open source → thehourglass.ai/finlay.
